title: Origins of Democracy and Republic
description: Trace democratic ideas from Athens and Rome through the Enlightenment to modern democracy.
objectives: Analyze Athenian democracy's strengths and limits
Trace the development of republican government
Connect historical governance to today's systems

lessons.title: Athens and Rome
lessons.content: Ancient Athens and Rome created enduring models of self-governance.
examples: Athens (Cleisthenes, ~508 BCE): direct democracy; 30,000 male citizens could vote; excluded women, slaves, foreigners
Pericles' Funeral Oration: 'power in the hands of the many, not the few'
Roman Republic: SPQR (Senatus Populusque Romanus); Senate, consuls, tribunes; model for the U.S. Constitution

lessons.title: Magna Carta to Enlightenment
lessons.content: English constitutional tradition slowly expanded rights and limited royal power.
examples: Magna Carta (1215): 'no taxation without representation' principle; habeas corpus
English Civil War and Glorious Revolution (1688): Parliamentary supremacy established
Locke, Montesquieu, Rousseau: Enlightenment thinkers who directly influenced the American Founders

title: U.S. History — The Gilded Age to WWI
description: Examine America's rise to world power from Reconstruction's end through WWI.
objectives: Describe the Gilded Age economy and its contradictions
Analyze American imperialism in Cuba, Philippines, and Panama
Explain U.S. entry into WWI

lessons.title: Gilded Age and Robber Barons
lessons.content: The Gilded Age (1870–1900) saw explosive economic growth alongside staggering inequality.
examples: Cornelius Vanderbilt (railroads), Andrew Carnegie (steel), John D. Rockefeller (oil): built monopolies worth hundreds of billions in today's dollars
Sherman Antitrust Act (1890): first attempt to regulate monopolies — largely unenforced
Workers formed unions: Knights of Labor, AFL; Homestead Strike (1892) and Pullman Strike (1894) crushed by force

lessons.title: American Imperialism
lessons.content: At the turn of the 20th century, the U.S. became an imperial power.
examples: Spanish-American War (1898): U.S. gained Guam, Puerto Rico, Philippines
Panama Canal (1904–1914): U.S. backed Panamanian independence from Colombia to secure canal rights
Yellow journalism (Hearst, Pulitzer): sensationalist coverage inflamed public opinion toward war

title: U.S. History — WWII Through Cold War
description: Examine the United States from WWII mobilization through the Cold War era.
objectives: Describe total war mobilization on the home front
Evaluate the decision to use atomic bombs
Analyze the domestic Cold War: McCarthyism and civil defense

lessons.title: WWII Home Front
lessons.content: WWII required the mobilization of the entire American economy and society.
examples: War Production Board: converted factories from consumer goods to weapons virtually overnight
6 million women entered the workforce ('Rosie the Riveter')
Japanese American internment: Executive Order 9066; 120,000 Japanese Americans sent to camps; later ruled unconstitutional
African American 'Double V' campaign: victory against fascism abroad AND Jim Crow at home

lessons.title: Atomic Bomb and Cold War
lessons.content: The atomic bomb ended WWII but began a new era of existential threat.
examples: Truman's decision: estimated 500,000–1 million U.S. casualties to invade Japan; actual deaths from bombs ~200,000
USSR tests atomic bomb (1949) → nuclear arms race
McCarthyism (1950–54): Senator McCarthy accused hundreds of communism with little evidence; damaged civil liberties

title: The Civil Rights Movement — Depth Study
description: Examine the Civil Rights Movement in depth, from its roots to its legislative victories.
objectives: Trace the legal and political strategy of the NAACP
Analyze key events and turning points
Evaluate the unfinished work of the movement

lessons.title: Legal Strategy — NAACP
lessons.content: The NAACP systematically challenged segregation through the courts.
examples: Thurgood Marshall argued 32 cases before the Supreme Court; won 29
Brown v. Board of Education (1954): overturned Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)
Strategy: challenge the 'separate but equal' doctrine by proving separate was inherently unequal

lessons.title: Street-Level Activism
lessons.content: Mass direct action combined with legal strategy to win legislative victories.
examples: Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–56): 381 days; MIA organized carpools; Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional
Birmingham Campaign (1963): Bull Connor's fire hoses and police dogs broadcast nationally → shocked the nation
March on Washington (August 28, 1963): 250,000 attended; MLK's 'I Have a Dream' speech
Selma to Montgomery March (1965) → Voting Rights Act (1965)

title: Social Movements of the 1960s–70s
description: Examine the major social movements that transformed American society in the 1960s–70s.
objectives: Describe the women's liberation movement
Analyze the environmental movement's origins
Evaluate the legacy of these movements

lessons.title: Women's Liberation Movement
lessons.content: Second-wave feminism challenged gender discrimination in law and culture.
examples: Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963): gave voice to educated women's dissatisfaction
NOW (National Organization for Women, 1966): lobbied for legal equality
Title IX (1972): banned sex discrimination in education → transformed women's athletics
Roe v. Wade (1973): abortion rights; remained law until overturned by Dobbs (2022)

lessons.title: Environmental Movement
lessons.content: The environmental movement transformed American law and consciousness.
examples: Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962): documented pesticide dangers; sparked the environmental movement
Cuyahoga River fire (1969): burning river in Cleveland shocked the nation
Earth Day (April 22, 1970): 20 million Americans participated
EPA established (1970); Clean Air Act (1970); Clean Water Act (1972)

title: America from Reagan to Obama
description: Survey American history from the Reagan Revolution through the Obama era.
objectives: Explain Reagan's political and economic philosophy
Describe post-Cold War American foreign policy
Analyze the significance of Obama's election

lessons.title: The Reagan Revolution
lessons.content: Ronald Reagan's presidency (1981–1989) shifted American politics rightward.
examples: Supply-side economics ('Reaganomics'): cut taxes especially for wealthy; deregulate business
'Evil Empire' speech: escalated Cold War rhetoric against USSR; Soviet economy couldn't keep up
Iran-Contra affair: administration secretly sold arms to Iran, used proceeds to fund Nicaraguan Contras (illegal)

lessons.title: Post-Cold War to Obama
lessons.content: Post-Cold War America faced new challenges and historic milestones.
examples: 1st Gulf War (1991): U.S. led coalition expelled Iraq from Kuwait
Clinton era: longest peacetime expansion; NAFTA; welfare reform; scandal and impeachment
9/11 and 'War on Terror': transformed foreign policy, civil liberties, and national psychology
Obama (2008): first Black president; ACA ('Obamacare'); 2009 Nobel Peace Prize; economy recovery from Great Recession

title: Global History — 20th Century Atrocities
description: Study 20th-century genocides and crimes against humanity and the international response.
objectives: Study the Armenian Genocide as a forerunner of the Holocaust
Analyze the Rwandan Genocide
Evaluate the effectiveness of 'Never Again'

lessons.title: Defining Genocide
lessons.content: Genocide is the deliberate destruction of a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group.
examples: Coined by Raphael Lemkin (1944) who lost 49 family members in the Holocaust
UN Genocide Convention (1948): first international law defining and prohibiting genocide
'Never Again': promise made after the Holocaust — but genocide has continued

lessons.title: Rwandan Genocide (1994)
lessons.content: 800,000 Tutsi were killed in 100 days while the world watched.
examples: Colonial Belgium had institutionalized Hutu-Tutsi distinction, exacerbating tensions
Radio broadcasts (RTLM) called Tutsi 'cockroaches' and incited killing
U.S. and UN explicitly avoided using the word 'genocide' to avoid obligation to intervene
International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda: held perpetrators accountable; established precedents for international justice

title: Globalization and its Discontents
description: Analyze globalization — its economic benefits, cultural impacts, and growing backlash.
objectives: Define economic globalization
Evaluate who benefits and who loses
Analyze the backlash to globalization

lessons.title: Economic Globalization
lessons.content: Since 1991, economic integration has accelerated dramatically.
examples: World trade tripled between 1990 and 2020
Global extreme poverty dropped from ~36% (1990) to ~10% (2015) — largely due to China's growth
Multinational corporations: Apple, Amazon, and Walmart each have revenues larger than most countries' GDPs

lessons.title: Globalization's Discontents
lessons.content: Globalization has created winners and losers — and fueled political backlash.
examples: Deindustrialization: manufacturing jobs moved to low-wage countries → rust belt economies in U.S., UK, France
'Race to the bottom': competition for jobs leads countries to weaken labor and environmental standards
Brexit (2016), Trump (2016), nationalism in France, Hungary: political backlash against globalization
Inequality within countries has grown even as inequality between countries shrinks

title: Technology and History
description: Analyze how transformative technologies have shaped historical change.
objectives: Identify key technologies that changed history
Analyze the printing press, industrial machinery, and the internet
Evaluate the current digital revolution

lessons.title: Technologies That Changed History
lessons.content: Certain inventions fundamentally altered the course of human history.
examples: Printing press (1440): enabled Reformation, Scientific Revolution, American Revolution — made ideas unstoppable
Steam engine (1769): Industrial Revolution; transformed work, cities, and global power
Internet (1991, public): democratized information; connected the world; enabled social media and disinformation

lessons.title: The Digital Revolution
lessons.content: We are living through a transformation as significant as the Industrial Revolution.
examples: AI revolution: automation threatens white-collar as well as blue-collar jobs
Social media: Arab Spring; Cambridge Analytica; social isolation; democracy under pressure
Big data and surveillance: governments and corporations can track behavior at unprecedented scale
The choices made in the next decade about AI and digital rights will shape the 21st century

title: Historiography — How We Know History
description: Study how history is written, interpreted, and contested.
objectives: Define historiography
Analyze how interpretations of history change over time
Evaluate primary sources for bias and context

lessons.title: What is Historiography?
lessons.content: Historiography is the study of how history is written and how interpretations change.
examples: The same event can be interpreted very differently by different historians
'History is written by the victors' — whose perspective is missing?
Revisionist history: when new evidence or perspectives change the accepted narrative (not a bad thing — it's how history improves)

lessons.title: Evaluating Sources
lessons.content: All historical sources have a perspective, audience, and purpose.
examples: HAPP analysis: Historical context, Audience, Purpose, Perspective
Primary source: letter from a Civil War soldier — invaluable but represents one person's limited view
The Diary of Anne Frank: extraordinary primary source, but unrepresentative of most Holocaust victims' experience
'Silences' in the archive: whose voices are missing? Why? What does that tell us?
